title: Ποσειδάωνος ἔφοδος
titleEn: Poseidon Comes to the Ships — Iliad 13.1–80
about: Zeus, having brought Hector and the Trojans to the ships, turns his eyes away to the northern peoples and does not expect any god to join the fight. But Poseidon is watching from a peak on Samothrace and pities the Achaeans, and he comes down the mountain, which shakes under his feet, and drives in four strides to his palace at Aegae. He takes his gold-maned horses, harnesses them, and rides over a parting sea to a cave between Tenedos and Imbros, where he hobbles them with golden fetters and leaves them to wait. The Trojans press on behind Hector like fire or a storm, sure of taking the ships. Poseidon, in the likeness of the seer Calchas, urges the two Ajaxes to stand firm, touches them with his staff, filling them with strength, and vanishes like a hawk. Ajax son of Oileus knows him by his footprints, and Telamonian Ajax feels the same eagerness to fight Hector.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν Τρῶάς τε καὶ Ἕκτορα νηυσὶ πέλασσε,
τοὺς μὲν ἔα παρὰ τῇσι πόνον τ’ ἐχέμεν καὶ ὀϊζὺν
νωλεμέως,
sentences.l:
And Zeus, when then both the Trojans and Hector near the ships he had brought,
those he let have beside them toil and distress
unceasingly,
sentences.i: Now when Zeus had brought Hector and the Trojans up to the ships, he left them there to have toil and distress without pause,
sentences.n: Zeus has done what he promised and now looks away. ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘when then’, and πέλασσε is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’, with νηυσί (dative) ‘to the ships’ as the goal and Τρῶας … καὶ Ἕκτορα as its objects. τοὺς μέν ‘those’ means the Trojans; ἔα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘let, leave’, followed by the infinitive ἐχέμεν (epic for ἔχειν) ‘to have’, with πόνον ‘toil’ and ὀϊζύν ‘distress’ as what they are left with. τῇσι is the article used as a pronoun, ‘them’, that is the ships, in the dative plural -ῃσι. νωλεμέως is ‘unceasingly’. The unit ends at the comma, because the sentence runs on for four more lines.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δὲ πάλιν τρέπεν ὄσσε φαεινὼ
νόσφιν ἐφ’ ἱπποπόλων Θρῃκῶν καθορώμενος αἶαν
Μυσῶν τ’ ἀγχεμάχων καὶ ἀγαυῶν ἱππημολγῶν
γλακτοφάγων Ἀβίων τε δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
but himself back he turned his two shining eyes
away, toward the horse-herding Thracians, looking down on the land
of the close-fighting Mysians and of the noble mare-milkers,
milk-eaters, and of the Abii, most just of men.
sentences.i: but he himself turned his shining eyes back and away, toward the horse-herding Thracians, looking down on the land of the close-fighting Mysians, of the noble mare-milkers, the milk-eaters, and of the Abii, the most just of men.
sentences.n: Zeus turns his eyes from Troy to the far north. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is Zeus; τρέπεν is an unaugmented imperfect of τρέπω ‘turn’, and ὄσσε φαεινώ is the dual, ‘his two shining eyes’. νόσφιν is ‘away’. νόσφιν ἐφ’ ἱπποπόλων Θρῃκῶν is ‘away toward the horse-herding Thracians’ (ἐπί with the genitive, of direction), and καθορώμενος is the middle participle of καθοράω, ‘looking down on’, active in sense, with αἶαν ‘land’ as its object; the peoples after it stand in the genitive depending on αἶαν. ἱπποπόλων ‘horse-herding’ is a compound whose second half is generally taken to mean ‘tending’; ἀγχεμάχων ‘close-fighting’ is from ἀγχί ‘near’ and μάχομαι ‘fight’; ἱππημολγῶν ‘mare-milkers’ is ἵππος ‘horse’ with ἀμέλγω ‘milk’, and γλακτοφάγων ‘milk-eating’ is from γάλα, γάλακτος ‘milk’ and the stem of φαγεῖν ‘eat’; ἀγαυῶν is ‘noble’. Whether the mare-milkers and the Abii are one people or two the Greek does not say, and the English keeps its list as loose as the Greek. δικαιοτάτων is the superlative of δίκαιος ‘just’.

sentences.t: ἐς Τροίην δ’ οὐ πάμπαν ἔτι τρέπεν ὄσσε φαεινώ·
sentences.l: And to Troy not at all any longer he turned his two shining eyes;
sentences.i: And he no longer turned his shining eyes to Troy at all;
sentences.n: Zeus keeps his eyes off Troy. ἐς Τροίην is ‘to Troy’ (Ionic -ην for -αν); οὐ πάμπαν ἔτι is ‘not at all any longer’. The verb and the dual ὄσσε φαεινώ repeat the words of line 3, and the unit ends at the ano teleia, since the next line gives the reason with γάρ.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀθανάτων τινα ἔλπετο ὃν κατὰ θυμὸν
ἐλθόντ’ ἢ Τρώεσσιν ἀρηξέμεν ἢ Δαναοῖσιν.
sentences.l:
for not he, of the immortals, anyone expected in his own heart
having come, either the Trojans to help or the Danaans.
sentences.i: for he did not expect in his own heart that any of the immortals would come to help either the Trojans or the Danaans.
sentences.n: Why Zeus can look away: he thinks no god will join in. ἔλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope, expect’, with the accusative τινα … ἐλθόντα, ‘that anyone, having come, …’ (ἀθανάτων τινα is ‘any of the immortals’), and the future infinitive ἀρηξέμεν ‘would help’, the epic form in -έμεν of ἀρήξειν (from ἀρήγω). ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in his own heart’, the possessive ὅς and not the relative. ἢ … ἢ is ‘either … or’; Δαναοῖσιν is the dative of Δαναοί ‘Danaans’.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχε κρείων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.l: Nor a blind man’s watch kept the lord earth-shaker;
sentences.i: Nor was the lord earth-shaker keeping a blind man’s watch;
sentences.n: Poseidon, not yet named, is watching. κρείων ἐνοσίχθων ‘the lord earth-shaker’ is the stock title for him; his name comes at line 19. ἀλαοσκοπιήν is ‘a blind man’s watch’, a watch kept by one who does not see, that is a careless one; the English keeps the picture (ἀλαός ‘blind’ + σκοπιή ‘watch’). εἶχε is the imperfect of ἔχω, ‘kept’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ὃ θαυμάζων ἧστο πτόλεμόν τε μάχην τε
ὑψοῦ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτης κορυφῆς Σάμου ὑληέσσης
Θρηϊκίης·
sentences.i: for he sat marvelling at the war and the fighting, high on the topmost peak of wooded Thracian Samos;
sentences.n: Where Poseidon sits and what holds him there. καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, and ὃ is ‘he’, Poseidon. θαυμάζων is ‘marvelling’, with the accusatives πτόλεμον τε μάχην τε ‘both war and fighting’ (πτόλεμος is the epic form of πόλεμος, and μάχη is kept as ‘fighting’); ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. ὑψοῦ is ‘on high’, and ἀκροτάτης is the superlative of ἄκρος, ‘topmost’. Σάμου ὑληέσσης Θρηϊκίης is ‘wooded Samos, the Thracian one’ (ὑληέσσης from ὕλη ‘forest’); this is the island of Samothrace, so called to tell it from the Samos off Asia Minor. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν γὰρ ἐφαίνετο πᾶσα μὲν Ἴδη,
φαίνετο δὲ Πριάμοιο πόλις καὶ νῆες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
for from there appeared all Ida,
and appeared Priam’s city and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: for from there all of Ida could be seen, and Priam’s city, and the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: What he can see from there. ἔνθεν is ‘from there’; ἐφαίνετο is the imperfect middle of φαίνω ‘show’, ‘was seen, appeared’, and φαίνετο is the same verb again at the start of the next line. πᾶσα μὲν Ἴδη … φαίνετο δὲ … is a ‘both … and’ pair (μέν … δέ): all of Ida, the mountain behind Troy, and the city and the ships. Πριάμοιο is the epic genitive of Πρίαμος.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἐξ ἁλὸς ἕζετ’ ἰών, ἐλέαιρε δ’ Ἀχαιοὺς
Τρωσὶν δαμναμένους, Διὶ δὲ κρατερῶς ἐνεμέσσα.
sentences.l:
There then he, out of the salt-sea, sat down, coming, and pitied the Achaeans
being subdued by the Trojans, and with Zeus strongly he felt resentment.
sentences.i: There he sat, come from the sea, and he pitied the Achaeans, who were being subdued by the Trojans, and felt strong resentment against Zeus.
sentences.n: Poseidon takes the Achaeans’ side. ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ is ‘there then’; ἕζετ’ is ἕζετο, the unaugmented imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’, and ἰών ‘coming’ goes with ἐξ ἁλός ‘out of the sea’, which says where he came from. ἐλέαιρε is the imperfect of ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’, with Ἀχαιούς as its object and δαμναμένους, the present passive participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’, ‘being subdued’, with the dative Τρωσίν (= Τρωσί) ‘by the Trojans’. ἐνεμέσσα is the imperfect of νεμεσάω (epic νεμεσσάω) ‘feel resentment’, with the dative Διί; κρατερῶς is ‘strongly’.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὄρεος κατεβήσετο παιπαλόεντος
κραιπνὰ ποσὶ προβιβάς·
sentences.l:
And at once from the mountain he came down, the rugged one,
at a rush with his feet, striding forward;
sentences.i: At once he came down from the rugged mountain, striding forward at a rush on his feet;
sentences.n: Poseidon leaves his seat on the mountain. αὐτίκα is ‘at once’. κατεβήσετο is the aorist middle of καταβαίνω, ‘came down’, in the -σετο form common in Homer; ἐξ ὄρεος παιπαλόεντος is ‘from the rugged mountain’ (ὄρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος, and παιπαλόεις ‘rugged’ is a word of uncertain origin). κραιπνά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘at a rush’; ποσί is ‘with his feet’, and προβιβάς is the participle of προβίβημι, ‘stride forward’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
τρέμε δ’ οὔρεα μακρὰ καὶ ὕλη
ποσσὶν ὑπ’ ἀθανάτοισι Ποσειδάωνος ἰόντος.
sentences.l:
and trembled the tall mountains and the forest
beneath the immortal feet of Poseidon as he went.
sentences.i: and the tall mountains and the forest trembled beneath the immortal feet of Poseidon as he went.
sentences.n: The mountains shake under him; this is the first place his name is given. τρέμε is the unaugmented imperfect of τρέμω ‘tremble’, with οὔρεα (the epic plural of ὄρος ‘mountain’) and ὕλη ‘forest’ as subjects, and μακρά ‘tall’ describing the mountains. ποσσὶν ὑπ’ ἀθανάτοισι is ‘beneath the immortal feet’, with ὑπό and the dative. Ποσειδάωνος ἰόντος is the genitive ‘of Poseidon going’, attached to the feet.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ὀρέξατ’ ἰών, τὸ δὲ τέτρατον ἵκετο τέκμωρ
Αἰγάς, ἔνθα δέ οἱ κλυτὰ δώματα βένθεσι λίμνης
χρύσεα μαρμαίροντα τετεύχαται ἄφθιτα αἰεί.
sentences.l:
Three times he stretched himself, going, and the fourth time he reached the end,
Aegae, where for him famous halls in the depths of the water
are golden, gleaming, made, unfailing for ever.
sentences.i: Three times he strode out as he went, and the fourth time he reached his journey’s end, Aegae, where his famous halls stand in the depths of the water, golden and gleaming, unfailing for ever.
sentences.n: Poseidon crosses to his home under the sea in four strides. ὀρέξατ’ is the aorist middle of ὀρέγω ‘reach, stretch out’; the picture is of a stride, which the Greek does not name. τὸ δὲ τέτρατον is ‘and the fourth time’, and τέκμωρ is ‘end, goal’, here the end of the journey. Αἰγάς is the place, in the accusative after ἵκετο ‘reached’; where it lies the Greek does not say beyond ‘in the depths of the water’. οἱ is the dative ‘for him’, κλυτά is ‘famous’, and βένθεσι is the dative plural of βένθος ‘depth’; λίμνης is the genitive of λίμνη, which is any standing or open water, here the sea. χρύσεα μαρμαίροντα is ‘golden, gleaming’, and τετεύχαται is the perfect passive of τεύχω, 3rd plural in the old -αται ending, ‘have been made’. ἄφθιτα ‘unfailing’ and αἰεί ‘for ever’ close the sentence.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐλθὼν ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι τιτύσκετο χαλκόποδ’ ἵππω
ὠκυπέτα χρυσέῃσιν ἐθείρῃσιν κομόωντε,
sentences.l:
There, having come, under the chariot he was making ready two bronze-footed horses,
swift-flying, with golden manes worn long,
sentences.i: There he came and harnessed to his chariot his two bronze-hoofed horses, swift of flight, with their long golden manes,
sentences.n: Poseidon harnesses his horses. ἔνθ’ ἐλθών is ‘having come there’, to Aegae; the rest of the two lines is word for word the harnessing of Zeus’s horses at 8.41–42, where ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ stands in its place. ὄχεσφι is the old -φι form of the plural of ὄχος ‘chariot’ (the plural is used for a single car), so ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι is ‘beneath the chariot’, that is, under its yoke; τιτύσκετο is the imperfect middle of τιτύσκομαι ‘make ready’. ἵππω is a dual, ‘two horses’, and so are the three words that agree with it: χαλκόποδ’ (χαλκόποδε) ‘bronze-footed’, ὠκυπέτα ‘swift-flying’ (ὠκύς ‘swift’ + πέτομαι ‘fly’), and κομόωντε, the dual of the participle of κομάω ‘wear the hair long’. χρυσέῃσιν ἐθείρῃσιν is the dative ‘with golden manes’.

sentences.t: χρυσὸν δ’ αὐτὸς ἔδυνε περὶ χροΐ,
sentences.l: and gold himself he put on about his skin,
sentences.i: and he himself put gold on about his body,
sentences.n: Poseidon dresses for the drive. χρυσόν is ‘gold’, standing for golden clothing or armour (the Greek does not say which); αὐτός ‘himself’ is Poseidon, and ἔδυνε is the imperfect of δύνω ‘put on’, with περὶ χροΐ ‘about his skin’, χροΐ being the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. These words are the first half of 8.43, and the unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
γέντο δ’ ἱμάσθλην
χρυσείην εὔτυκτον,
sentences.l:
and took up a lash,
golden, well-made,
sentences.i: and took up a golden lash, well made,
sentences.n: He takes up the lash. γέντο is an aorist of a verb that has no present, ‘took up, grasped’, with δ’ ‘and’. ἱμάσθλην is ‘a lash’, χρυσείην ‘golden’ and εὔτυκτον ‘well-made’, both agreeing with it; the adjective χρυσείην is placed at the start of the next line, away from its noun. These are the words of 8.43–44.

sentences.t: ἑοῦ δ’ ἐπεβήσετο δίφρου,
sentences.l: and mounted his own chariot,
sentences.i: and mounted his chariot,
sentences.n: He mounts. ἑοῦ is the reflexive possessive ‘his own’, agreeing with δίφρου ‘chariot’; ἐπεβήσετο is the aorist middle of ἐπιβαίνω, ‘mounted’, which takes a genitive. The ‘and’ δ’ joins this to the lash he has just taken; the words are those of 8.44, and the unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἐλάαν ἐπὶ κύματ’·
sentences.l: and he went to drive over the waves;
sentences.i: and set out to drive over the waves;
sentences.n: He sets out over the sea. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, with the infinitive ἐλάαν (from ἐλαύνω ‘drive’) giving what he went to do; ἐπὶ κύματα is ‘over the waves’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἄταλλε δὲ κήτε’ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ
πάντοθεν ἐκ κευθμῶν, οὐδ’ ἠγνοίησεν ἄνακτα·
sentences.l:
and frolicked the sea-monsters beneath him
from every side out of their hiding-places, and did not fail to recognize their lord;
sentences.i: and the sea-monsters came frolicking out of their recesses on every side beneath him, and did not fail to know their lord;
sentences.n: The creatures of the sea greet him. ἄταλλε is the imperfect of ἀτάλλω ‘skip, frolic’, with κήτε’ (κήτεα, the plural of κῆτος ‘sea-monster’) as subject; a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb. ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘beneath him’, πάντοθεν ‘from every side’, and κευθμῶν the genitive plural of κευθμός ‘hiding-place’ (from κεύθω ‘hide’). οὐδ’ ἠγνοίησεν is ‘and did not fail to recognize’, the aorist of ἀγνοιέω ‘not know’, with ἄνακτα ‘lord’, Poseidon.

sentences.t: γηθοσύνῃ δὲ θάλασσα διίστατο·
sentences.l: and for joy the sea parted;
sentences.i: and the sea parted for joy;
sentences.n: The sea makes way. γηθοσύνῃ is the dative ‘with joy’ (from γηθοσύνη, related to γηθέω ‘rejoice’); θάλασσα is ‘the sea’, and διίστατο is the imperfect of διίσταμαι ‘stand apart’, ‘parted’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ πέτοντο
ῥίμφα μάλ’, οὐδ’ ὑπένερθε διαίνετο χάλκεος ἄξων·
sentences.l:
and they flew
very nimbly, and beneath was not wetted the bronze axle;
sentences.i: and they flew on very nimbly, and the bronze axle below was not wetted;
sentences.n: The horses skim the surface. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, the horses (plural here, not the dual), and πέτοντο is an unaugmented imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’. ῥίμφα ‘nimbly’ is an adverb, strengthened by μάλ’ (μάλα) ‘very’; ὑπένερθε is ‘underneath’, and διαίνετο is the imperfect passive of διαίνω ‘wet’. χάλκεος ἄξων is ‘the bronze axle’; the picture is of a car so light on the water that the axle stays dry.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐς Ἀχαιῶν νῆας ἐΰσκαρθμοι φέρον ἵπποι.
sentences.l: and him to the ships of the Achaeans well-bounding carried the horses.
sentences.i: and the well-bounding horses carried him to the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: He arrives at the Achaean camp. τόν ‘him’ is Poseidon, with the article as a pronoun; ἐς … νῆας is ‘to the ships’. ἐΰσκαρθμοι is ‘well-bounding’, from ἐΰ ‘well’ and, apparently, a noun for ‘leap’ related to σκαίρω ‘skip, bound’. φέρον is an unaugmented imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’, and ἵπποι ‘horses’ is the subject, placed last.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τι σπέος εὐρὺ βαθείης βένθεσι λίμνης
μεσσηγὺς Τενέδοιο καὶ Ἴμβρου παιπαλοέσσης·
sentences.l:
And there is a certain cave, wide, in the depths of the deep water
between Tenedos and rugged Imbros;
sentences.i: There is a wide cave in the depths of the deep water, between Tenedos and rugged Imbros;
sentences.n: Poseidon’s stable. A new paragraph begins here. ἔστι δέ τι is ‘and there is a certain’, with σπέος ‘cave’ and εὐρύ ‘wide’. βαθείης … λίμνης is ‘of the deep water’ and βένθεσι ‘in the depths’, as in line 21. μεσσηγύς ‘between’ takes the genitives Τενέδοιο and Ἴμβρου, Tenedos and Imbros, two islands in the north-east Aegean; παιπαλοέσσης ‘rugged’ is the feminine of the παιπαλόεις of line 17.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἵππους ἔστησε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων
λύσας ἐξ ὀχέων,
sentences.l:
there the horses stopped Poseidon earth-shaker,
having loosed them from the chariot,
sentences.i: there Poseidon earth-shaker stopped his horses, and loosed them from the chariot,
sentences.n: He unyokes them. ἔνθ’ is ἔνθα ‘there’, and ἔστησε is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stop’, here transitive. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘Poseidon earth-shaker’, the stock pair. λύσας ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘having loosed (them) from the chariot’, with ὀχέων the genitive plural of ὄχος. The same pattern is used of Zeus at 8.49. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
παρὰ δ’ ἀμβρόσιον βάλεν εἶδαρ
ἔδμεναι·
sentences.l:
and beside them he cast ambrosial food
to eat;
sentences.i: and threw ambrosial food down beside them to eat;
sentences.n: He feeds them. παρά is an adverb, ‘beside (them)’, and βάλεν the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, ‘threw’. ἀμβρόσιον εἶδαρ is ‘ambrosial food’, the fodder of immortal horses; ἔδμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἔδω ‘eat’ (= Attic ἐσθίειν), ‘to eat’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ ποσσὶ πέδας ἔβαλε χρυσείας
ἀρρήκτους ἀλύτους, ὄφρ’ ἔμπεδον αὖθι μένοιεν
νοστήσαντα ἄνακτα·
sentences.i: and put golden fetters around their feet, that could not be broken or undone, so that they would stay fast right there until their lord came back;
sentences.n: He hobbles them so that they will wait. ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’, and ποσσί ‘feet’ is the dative of the place; πέδας is ‘fetters’ and χρυσείας ‘golden’. ἀρρήκτους ἀλύτους is ‘unbreakable, not to be undone’ (negative α- with ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ and with λύω ‘loose’); the whole line 37 is the line that describes Hephaestus’ bonds at Odyssey 8.275. ὄφρα with the optative μένοιεν is ‘so that they would stay’, a purpose clause after a past verb; ἔμπεδον is ‘firmly’ and αὖθι ‘on the spot’. νοστήσαντα ἄνακτα, ‘their lord having returned’, is the object of μένοιεν, which here means ‘wait for’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 38.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐς στρατὸν ᾤχετ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: and he went off to the army of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and he went off to the army of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Poseidon goes to the Achaeans. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’; ᾤχετ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go off’, and ἐς στρατὸν … Ἀχαιῶν is ‘to the army of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ φλογὶ ἶσοι ἀολλέες ἠὲ θυέλλῃ
Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ ἄμοτον μεμαῶτες ἕποντο
ἄβρομοι αὐΐαχοι·
sentences.i: And the Trojans, in a close mass, like flame or a storm-blast, followed Hector, son of Priam, eager without ceasing, roaring and shouting;
sentences.n: The Trojans’ charge. A new paragraph begins here. φλογὶ ἶσοι ἠὲ θυέλλῃ is ‘equal to flame or to a storm’, with ἶσος taking the dative, and ἠέ ‘or’ joining the two; θύελλα is a storm-wind, kept as ‘storm-blast’. ἀολλέες is ‘in a close mass’. ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, with the dative Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ ‘Hector, Priam’s son’ (a patronymic). μεμαῶτες is the perfect participle of μάομαι, ‘eager’, and with ἄμοτον it is ‘eager without ceasing’; the sense of ἄμοτον is not known, and ‘unceasingly’ is the traditional guess. ἄβρομοι αὐΐαχοι ‘roaring, shouting’ are two words whose make-up is not secure (the first seems to be built on βρόμος ‘roar’); the English is a guess at both. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 41.

sentences.t:
ἔλποντο δὲ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
αἱρήσειν, κτενέειν δὲ παρ’ αὐτόθι πάντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.l:
and they expected the ships of the Achaeans
to take, and to kill on the spot all the best.
sentences.i: and they expected to take the ships of the Achaeans and to kill all their best men right there on the spot.
sentences.n: What the Trojans hope for. ἔλποντο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope, expect’, and the two future infinitives that follow, αἱρήσειν ‘to take’ (from αἱρέω) and κτενέειν (the uncontracted future of κτείνω ‘kill’, Attic κτενεῖν), say what they expect. παρ’ αὐτόθι is ‘there, on the very spot’; πάντας ἀρίστους is ‘all the best’, the best men of the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Ποσειδάων γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος
Ἀργείους ὄτρυνε βαθείης ἐξ ἁλὸς ἐλθὼν
εἰσάμενος Κάλχαντι δέμας καὶ ἀτειρέα φωνήν·
sentences.l:
But Poseidon, the earth-holder, the earth-shaker,
urged on the Argives, out of the deep salt-sea having come,
making himself like Calchas in body and in unwearied voice:
sentences.i: But Poseidon the earth-holder, the earth-shaker came from the deep sea and urged on the Argives, taking the likeness of Calchas in body and in his unwearied voice:
sentences.n: Poseidon, in disguise, rouses the Achaeans. γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος is ‘the earth-holder, the earth-shaker’, two stock epithets of Poseidon (γαῖα ‘earth’ with ἔχω ‘hold’, and with a word for ‘shake’), translated every time. Ἀργείους is ‘Argives’, one of the three names the poet gives the army. ὄτρυνε is the unaugmented past tense of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’; βαθείης ἐξ ἁλός ἐλθών is ‘having come from the deep sea’. εἰσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’, with the dative Κάλχαντι ‘to Calchas’, the Achaeans’ seer, and the accusatives of respect δέμας ‘in body’ and ἀτειρέα φωνήν ‘in unwearied voice’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: Αἴαντε πρώτω προσέφη μεμαῶτε καὶ αὐτώ·
sentences.l: The two Ajaxes first he addressed, both eager, of themselves too:
sentences.i: He spoke to the two Ajaxes first, both of them eager of their own accord:
sentences.n: Poseidon speaks to the two Ajaxes. Αἴαντε is a dual, ‘the two Ajaxes’ (Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus, who fight side by side), and πρώτω ‘first’, μεμαῶτε ‘eager’ and αὐτώ ‘themselves’ are duals agreeing with it. καὶ αὐτώ is ‘even themselves’, that is, already eager before he spoke. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘addressed’. The speech that follows (47–58) is Poseidon’s, in the likeness of Calchas.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντε σφὼ μέν τε σαώσετε λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
ἀλκῆς μνησαμένω, μὴ δὲ κρυεροῖο φόβοιο.
sentences.l:
“Two Ajaxes, you two will save the people of the Achaeans
if mindful of might, and not of chilling flight.
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, you two will save the army of the Achaeans, if you call to mind your might and not chilling flight.
sentences.n: Poseidon’s speech begins. Αἴαντε is the dual vocative, with σφώ ‘you two’ and the particles μέν τε ‘indeed’. σαώσετε is the future of σαόω ‘save’, a plural ending though only two are meant. μνησαμένω is the dual aorist middle participle of μιμνῄσκω, ‘having called to mind’ (the middle ‘remember’), taking a genitive: ἀλκῆς ‘of might’ and, after μὴ δέ ‘and not’, κρυεροῖο φόβοιο ‘of chilling flight’ (κρυερός ‘chilling’ is from κρύος ‘frost’; φόβος is the running of fear). The participle is conditional (‘if you remember’): they will save the army only if they are mindful of might.

sentences.t:
ἄλλῃ μὲν γὰρ ἔγωγ’ οὐ δείδια χεῖρας ἀάπτους
Τρώων, οἳ μέγα τεῖχος ὑπερκατέβησαν ὁμίλῳ·
sentences.l:
For elsewhere I do not fear the invincible hands
of the Trojans, who the great wall have gone down over in a throng;
sentences.i: For elsewhere I do not fear the invincible hands of the Trojans, who have come over the great wall in a throng;
sentences.n: Poseidon says where he is not afraid. ἄλλῃ μέν is ‘elsewhere’, answered by τῇ δέ in line 52; ἔγωγε is ‘I for my part’. δείδια is the perfect of δείδω, a present in sense, ‘I fear’, with the accusative χεῖρας ἀάπτους, ‘untouchable hands’; the meaning of ἀάπτους is not known, and ‘invincible’ is only a guess (another is ‘untouchable’, from ἅπτω ‘touch’). Τρώων is ‘of the Trojans’, and οἳ is the relative ‘who’. ὑπερκατέβησαν is the aorist of ὑπερκαταβαίνω ‘go down over’, with the accusative τεῖχος ‘wall’; ὁμίλῳ is ‘in a throng’. The wall is the Achaean camp’s.

sentences.t: ἕξουσιν γὰρ πάντας ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l: for will hold them all the well-greaved Achaeans;
sentences.i: for the well-greaved Achaeans will hold them all back;
sentences.n: Why he is not afraid there. ἕξουσιν is the future of ἔχω, here ‘will hold in check’, with πάντας ‘all’ as its object, the Trojans, who are not named in this line. ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock phrase for the army (the κνημίς is the greave that covers the shin); the diaeresis on ϋ is as the edition prints it.

sentences.t:
τῇ δὲ δὴ αἰνότατον περιδείδια μή τι πάθωμεν,
ᾗ ῥ’ ὅ γ’ ὁ λυσσώδης φλογὶ εἴκελος ἡγεμονεύει
Ἕκτωρ, ὃς Διὸς εὔχετ’ ἐρισθενέος πάϊς εἶναι.
sentences.l:
but there indeed most dreadfully I greatly fear lest we suffer something,
where that frenzied one, like to flame, leads,
Hector, who boasts to be the son of Zeus, of great strength.
sentences.i: but there I am most dreadfully afraid that we may suffer something, where that frenzied man, like flame, is leading: Hector, who claims to be the son of Zeus, great in strength.
sentences.n: Where he is afraid: where Hector leads. τῇ δὲ δή is ‘but there indeed’; αἰνότατον is the neuter superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’, used as an adverb, ‘most dreadfully’; περιδείδια is δείδια with περί ‘exceedingly’. μή τι πάθωμεν is a clause of fear, with the aorist subjunctive of πάσχω, ‘lest we suffer anything’. ᾗ ῥ’ is ‘where indeed’; ὅ γε is ‘he’, and ὁ λυσσώδης is ‘the frenzied one’ (from λύσσα ‘wild frenzy’). φλογὶ εἴκελος is ‘like flame’, and ἡγεμονεύει ‘leads’. Ἕκτωρ stands in apposition. ὃς … εὔχετ’ … εἶναι is ‘who claims to be’; πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς ‘child, son’, and ἐρισθενέος is the genitive of ἐρισθενής ‘great in strength’, agreeing with Διός. The unit ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊν δ’ ὧδε θεῶν τις ἐνὶ φρεσὶ ποιήσειεν
αὐτώ θ’ ἑστάμεναι κρατερῶς καὶ ἀνωγέμεν ἄλλους·
sentences.l:
And for you two thus may one of the gods in your wits put it,
yourselves to stand strongly and to bid the others;
sentences.i: And may one of the gods so put it in the minds of you two to stand your own ground strongly, and to bid the others do the same;
sentences.n: Poseidon wishes the Ajaxes the will to stand. σφῶϊν is the dual dative ‘to you two’, and ὧδε ‘thus’. θεῶν τις is ‘one of the gods’. ποιήσειεν is the aorist optative of ποιέω, a wish, ‘may he make, put’; ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in the wits’, and the infinitives that follow say what he is to put there: αὐτώ θ’ ἑστάμεναι κρατερῶς ‘yourselves to stand strongly’ (αὐτώ is the dual ‘you two yourselves’; ἑστάμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἵστημι, here ‘stand’), and ἀνωγέμεν ἄλλους ‘to bid the others’ (ἀνωγέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἄνωγα ‘bid’). What the others are to be bidden is not said, and ‘do the same’ is the evident sense. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τώ κε καὶ ἐσσύμενόν περ ἐρωήσαιτ’ ἀπὸ νηῶν
ὠκυπόρων, εἰ καί μιν Ὀλύμπιος αὐτὸς ἐγείρει.
sentences.l:
then you might even drive him back, hurrying though he be, from the ships
swift-faring, even if the Olympian himself rouses him.”
sentences.i: then you might drive him back from the swift-faring ships, hurrying on as he is, even if the Olympian himself is rousing him.”
sentences.n: What that would achieve. τώ is ‘then, in that case’; κε … ἐρωήσαιτ’ is a potential optative (‘you might’) of ἐρωέω ‘draw back’, here transitive, ‘drive back’, with a plural ending for the two. ἐσσύμενον περ is ‘though hurrying’, the participle of σεύω in the passive with concessive περ; its noun is μιν ‘him’, Hector. ἀπὸ νηῶν ὠκυπόρων is ‘from the swift-faring ships’. εἰ καί is ‘even if’; Ὀλύμπιος αὐτός ‘the Olympian himself’ is Zeus, and ἐγείρει is ‘rouses’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ σκηπανίῳ γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος
ἀμφοτέρω κεκοπὼς πλῆσεν μένεος κρατεροῖο,
γυῖα δ’ ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρὰ πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and with a staff the earth-holder, the earth-shaker
striking the two of them filled them with strong fury,
and made their limbs light, the feet below and the hands above.
sentences.i: So he said, and the earth-holder, the earth-shaker struck the two of them with his staff and filled them with strong fury, and made their limbs light, their feet below and their hands above.
sentences.n: Poseidon touches the Ajaxes and gives them strength. A new paragraph begins here. ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, ἦ being a past form of the verb ‘say’. σκηπανίῳ is the dative of σκηπάνιον, ‘staff’, a rare word. γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος is the stock pair of line 43. ἀμφοτέρω is a dual accusative, ‘both’, and κεκοπώς is the perfect participle of κόπτω ‘strike’. πλῆσεν is the aorist of πίμπλημι ‘fill’, with the genitive μένεος κρατεροῖο, ‘with strong fury’ (μένος is impetuous fury). γυῖα is ‘limbs’ and ἐλαφρά ‘light’, with πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ‘as to feet and hands’; ὕπερθεν is ‘above’ and goes with the hands, the feet being understood as below (line 75 says so).

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ὥς τ’ ἴρηξ ὠκύπτερος ὦρτο πέτεσθαι,
ὅς ῥά τ’ ἀπ’ αἰγίλιπος πέτρης περιμήκεος ἀρθεὶς
ὁρμήσῃ πεδίοιο διώκειν ὄρνεον ἄλλο,
sentences.l:
And he himself, like a hawk, swift-winged, rose to fly,
which from a sheer rock, very tall, having been lifted,
may dart over the plain to chase another bird,
sentences.i: And he himself rose to fly like a swift-winged hawk, which, rising from a sheer and very tall rock, darts out over the plain to chase another bird,
sentences.n: Poseidon vanishes, and the poet gives a simile. αὐτός is Poseidon. ὥς τ’ is ‘just like’; ἴρηξ is ‘hawk’ and ὠκύπτερος ‘swift-winged’ (ὠκύς ‘swift’ + πτερόν ‘wing’); ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rose’, with the infinitive πέτεσθαι ‘to fly’. The relative clause that follows describes the hawk in general: ὅς ῥά τ’ with the subjunctive ὁρμήσῃ (aorist of ὁρμάω ‘dart, start’) gives the sense ‘as one does whenever it darts’. αἰγίλιπος is a rare word of unknown meaning, perhaps ‘left by goats’; ‘sheer’ is a guess. περιμήκεος is ‘very tall’ (περι- ‘very’ + μῆκος ‘length’), and ἀρθείς the aorist passive participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, ‘raised up’. πεδίοιο is ‘over the plain’, a genitive of the ground covered, and διώκειν ‘to chase’. ὄρνεον ἄλλο is ‘another bird’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀπὸ τῶν ἤϊξε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων.
sentences.l: so from them darted away Poseidon earth-shaker.
sentences.i: so Poseidon earth-shaker darted away from them.
sentences.n: The simile is closed. ὣς ‘so’ answers ὥς τ’ of line 62. ἀπὸ τῶν is ‘from them’, the Ajaxes, with τῶν the article as a pronoun; ἤϊξε is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is the stock pair.

sentences.t:
τοῖιν δ’ ἔγνω πρόσθεν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας,
αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Αἴαντα προσέφη Τελαμώνιον υἱόν·
sentences.l:
Of the two of them knew first swift Ajax, son of Oileus,
and at once then Ajax he addressed, the Telamonian son:
sentences.i: Of the two of them, swift Ajax, son of Oileus, was the first to know him, and at once he spoke to Ajax, Telamon’s son:
sentences.n: The sons of Oileus and Telamon share the next lines. τοῖιν is the dual of the pronoun, ‘of the two’, a partitive genitive; ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, with the god understood as its object; πρόσθεν is ‘before’, so ‘first’. Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας is ‘swift Ajax, son of Oileus’, the stock way of telling him from the other Ajax, and the genitive is his father’s name. αἶψα is ‘at once’, and προσέφη ‘addressed’. Αἴαντα … Τελαμώνιον υἱόν is ‘Ajax, Telamon’s son’, the other Ajax, with Τελαμώνιον ‘Telamonian’ agreeing with υἱόν, split by the verb.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν ἐπεί τις νῶϊ θεῶν οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι
μάντεϊ εἰδόμενος κέλεται παρὰ νηυσὶ μάχεσθαι,
οὐδ’ ὅ γε Κάλχας ἐστὶ θεοπρόπος οἰωνιστής·
sentences.i: “Ajax, since one of the gods who hold Olympus, taking the likeness of a seer, is bidding the two of us fight beside the ships, and he is not Calchas, the diviner, the reader of birds;
sentences.n: Ajax son of Oileus speaks. Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας. ἐπεί is ‘since’, and its clause runs to the ano teleia, without a main verb of its own; the proofs that follow (71–75) do that work. τις … θεῶν οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι is ‘some one of the gods who hold Olympus’. νῶϊ is the dual accusative ‘us two’, and μάντεϊ εἰδόμενος is ‘likening himself to a seer’ (εἰδόμενος is the participle of εἴδομαι ‘seem like’; μάντεϊ the dative of μάντις ‘seer’). κέλεται is ‘bids’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’. οὐδ’ ὅ γε Κάλχας ἐστί is ‘and he is not Calchas’; θεοπρόπος is ‘diviner’ and οἰωνιστής ‘reader of birds’ (from οἰωνός ‘bird of omen’).

sentences.t:
ἴχνια γὰρ μετόπισθε ποδῶν ἠδὲ κνημάων
ῥεῖ’ ἔγνων ἀπιόντος·
sentences.l:
for the tracks behind, of his feet and of his shins,
easily I knew, as he went away;
sentences.i: for I easily knew the tracks behind him, of his feet and of his shins, as he went away;
sentences.n: The first proof that the speaker was a god. ἴχνια is ‘tracks’; μετόπισθε ‘behind’; ποδῶν ἠδὲ κνημάων is ‘of feet and of shins’ (κνημάων is the Homeric genitive plural of κνήμη ‘shin’). ῥεῖ’ is ῥεῖα ‘easily’, an adverb, and ἔγνων the aorist ‘I recognised’. ἀπιόντος is the genitive of the participle of ἄπειμι ‘go away’, agreeing with the ‘him’ implied in ποδῶν … κνημάων. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 72.

sentences.t: ἀρίγνωτοι δὲ θεοί περ·
sentences.l: and easily known are gods, indeed;
sentences.i: and gods are easily recognised;
sentences.n: Why he could tell. ἀρίγνωτοι is ‘easily known’ (the prefix ἀρι- is intensive), agreeing with θεοί ‘gods’, and the verb ‘are’ is understood. περ adds emphasis, ‘gods indeed’; the point is that a god is not hard to know for one who looks.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι
μᾶλλον ἐφορμᾶται πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι,
μαιμώωσι δ’ ἔνερθε πόδες καὶ χεῖρες ὕπερθε.
sentences.l:
and in me myself too the heart within my dear chest
the more is impelled to wage war and to fight,
and they rage below, the feet, and above, the hands.”
sentences.i: and in me myself too the heart in my own chest is the more impelled to wage war and to fight, and my feet below and my hands above are raging.”
sentences.n: The second proof: the speaker feels the god’s touch. καὶ δ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ is ‘and in me myself too’. ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι is ‘within my dear chest’ (φίλος ‘dear’ with a part of the body means little more than ‘my own’); μᾶλλον ‘the more’. ἐφορμᾶται is the present of ἐφορμάομαι, ‘rush at, be impelled’, with the infinitives πολεμίζειν ‘to wage war’ and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ (ἠδέ ‘and’). μαιμώωσι is an uncontracted epic form (for μαιμῶσι) of μαιμάω ‘rage’, with πόδες ‘feet’ and χεῖρες ‘hands’ as subjects; ἔνερθε ‘below’ and ὕπερθε ‘above’ answer ὕπερθεν of line 61 (the feet and hands Poseidon made light). The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: In answer Telamonian Ajax said to him:
sentences.n: Telamonian Ajax answers. A new paragraph begins here. τόν ‘him’ is the other Ajax (the article as a pronoun); ἀπαμειβόμενος is the middle participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘addressed’. Τελαμώνιος Αἴας ‘Telamonian Ajax’ is the stock pair that tells him from the Ajax son of Oileus.

sentences.t:
οὕτω νῦν καὶ ἐμοὶ περὶ δούρατι χεῖρες ἄαπτοι
μαιμῶσιν, καί μοι μένος ὤρορε, νέρθε δὲ ποσσὶν
ἔσσυμαι ἀμφοτέροισι·
sentences.i: “So it is with me too now: my invincible hands are raging about my spear, and my fury has been roused, and below I am hurrying on both my feet;
sentences.n: Telamonian Ajax says he feels the same. οὕτω νῦν καί is ‘so now also’; ἐμοί is ‘to me’. περὶ δούρατι is ‘about the spear’ (περί with the dative), the spear he holds. χεῖρες ἄαπτοι is ‘invincible hands’, as at 49, where the note says the meaning of ἄαπτος is not known; the English gives the same guess. μαιμῶσιν is the contracted form of the verb of 75, ‘rage’. ὤρορε is the reduplicated aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’; whether μένος is its object (with a subject the Greek does not state) or its subject (‘fury has risen’) is disputed, and ‘has been roused’ keeps the subject unsaid and the question open. νέρθε is ἔνερθε ‘below’, and ποσσὶν … ἀμφοτέροισι ‘with both feet’ is split by the line end. ἔσσυμαι is the perfect passive of σεύω, ‘I am hurrying’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 79.

sentences.t:
μενοινώω δὲ καὶ οἶος
Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ ἄμοτον μεμαῶτι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and I yearn, even alone,
to fight Hector, Priam’s-son, unceasingly eager.”
sentences.i: and I yearn, even alone, to fight Hector, son of Priam, who is eager without ceasing.”
sentences.n: He wants to face Hector alone. μενοινώω is the uncontracted epic form (for μενοινῶ) of μενοινάω ‘have a mind to, yearn’. καὶ οἶος is ‘even alone’, with the nominative οἶος ‘alone’ agreeing with the speaker. μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ takes the dative Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ ‘Hector, Priam’s son’, and ἄμοτον μεμαῶτι ‘eager without ceasing’ agrees with Ἕκτορι, as at 40. The speech ends here, and with it the part.
